rationale: A wins because it keeps the heat without turning the unknowns into facts. Its line, "The refusal to split cuts from unfilled roles is part of the story, not a footnote," is the actual tension. B has real bones, but "the Equivalent of 700 People Are Gone" is exactly how a useful labor angle becomes a correction waiting to happen.
gaps_in_A: "how many people lost their jobs" pushes past the fact pattern; the update says headcount fell and Klarna will not split cuts from unfilled roles.
"a chatbot may be the first one to rule on it" is too assertive for facts that only say advocates raised concerns about AI handling disputes.
"The reporter will write this story with or without Klarna" is newsroom cosplay unless there are named advocates, complaints, or a regulator already moving.
gaps_in_B: "the Equivalent of 700 People Are Gone" is wrong. The update says the assistant handled equivalent work, not that 700 people disappeared.
"How Many Customer-Service Jobs It Eliminated" and "The Headcount It Cut Is the Margin It's Showing Investors" assert layoffs and investor messaging the update does not prove.
"advocacy concerns surfacing now are likely to precede regulatory attention" invents a regulatory peg. Concerns are in the update; impending regulatory attention is not.
"Before this, AI-in-customer-service claims were largely vendor-produced" is unsupported market context dressed up as fact. Cut it or prove it.
